title: Identity Life Cycle Management

header.html: 3.1 Understand identity life cycle management: Roles definition; Provision; Review; Deprovision; Frameworks and tools
the official ISC2 CC exam outline

html:
1The identity life cycle

An identity is the digital representation of a person, device, application or service. The life cycle follows it from creation to removal.

Stage What happens Why it matters
1 Roles definition Decide which roles exist and which access each role needs Access follows the job, not the person
2 Provision Create the account and grant the role's access when someone joins Right access on day one, approved by the owner
3 Review Check periodically that access is still needed (an access review or recertification) Stops privilege creep
4 Deprovision Disable and remove accounts and access when someone leaves or no longer needs it Closes the door on former staff

The cycle is often called joiner, mover, leaver: a mover gets new access and loses the old access.

Exam tip

. Roles first, then provision, review, deprovision. Disable accounts at once when someone leaves, and record who approved each grant.

2Privilege creep and orphaned accounts

Problem Meaning Fix
Privilege creep A person collects permissions over the years as they change jobs Access reviews and removing old rights when someone moves
Orphaned account An account with no active owner (the owner left) Deprovision at departure; find them by reviews
Dormant account An account that is not used Disable after a set period
Shared account Several people use one login Avoid: actions cannot be tied to a person
Exam tip

. Privilege creep is cured by access reviews and by removing the old rights when a person moves. Disable first, delete later, so that records stay for audit.

3Nonhuman identities, including AI

Service accounts, applications, devices and AI bots are identities too. They need the same life cycle:

Stage For a bot or service account
Roles definition Define what it may do (least privilege)
Provision Create it with an owner and store secrets safely
Review Check that it is still needed and that its rights are minimal
Deprovision Remove it and rotate its keys when the system is retired
Exam tip

. Every identity needs an owner, including bots. An AI bot with broad rights and no owner is an orphaned, over-privileged identity.

4Frameworks and tools

Tool What it does
Identity and access management (IAM) The overall discipline and tools that manage identities and access
Directory service (for example LDAP, Active Directory) Central store of identities and groups
Single sign-on (SSO) One login for many applications
Federation (SAML, OpenID Connect, OAuth) Trust between organizations, so identities are reused across them
Identity governance and administration (IGA) Automates provisioning, access requests and reviews
Privileged access management (PAM) Controls and records the use of powerful accounts
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) Stronger proof of identity

Tie the system to HR: a hire, move or exit event in the HR system should trigger provisioning or deprovisioning automatically.

5Exam Q&A

5.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1An employee leaves the company. What is the best first step for the access of this person?

  • AWait one month in case the person returns
  • BReduce the permissions of the person slowly
  • CDisable the accounts and access at once
  • DKeep the accounts for the next new hire
Show the answer

Answer: C. Deprovisioning must happen promptly so that former staff cannot keep access.

S2A person has worked in four departments and still has the permissions of all four. What is this problem called?

  • AFederation of identities across companies
  • BSingle sign-on across several different applications
  • CPrivilege creep from accumulated permissions
  • DSeparation of duties between departments
Show the answer

Answer: C. Accumulated permissions over time are privilege creep; access reviews and removal at job moves fix it.

S3Managers are asked every quarter to confirm that their team members still need their access. What is this process?

  • AProvisioning of new accounts
  • BAccess review, also called recertification
  • CDeprovisioning of former staff
  • DRoles definition for new jobs
Show the answer

Answer: B. Periodic confirmation that access is still needed is an access review.

S4Which stage of the identity life cycle decides what access a job needs before any account is created?

  • ADeprovision, which removes accounts
  • BReview, which checks existing access
  • CProvision, which creates the account
  • DRoles definition, which sets the access of a role
Show the answer

Answer: D. Roles definition comes first and describes the access each role needs.

S5An AI bot that reads customer files still runs after the project that created it ended, and no one owns it. What is the best description?

  • AAn orphaned, nonhuman identity that should be removed
  • BA secure service with no risk to the data
  • CA federated identity with a trusted partner
  • DA privileged administrator with a clear owner
Show the answer

Answer: A. Bots and service accounts are identities that need an owner and a life cycle; this one should be deprovisioned.

S6A company wants new staff accounts to be created automatically when HR records a hire. Which tool category supports this?

  • ANetwork intrusion prevention
  • BEndpoint disk encryption
  • CIdentity governance and administration
  • DData loss prevention for email
Show the answer

Answer: C. Identity governance and administration automates provisioning, requests and reviews based on HR events.

5.2 Recall questions

R1Name the four stages of the identity life cycle.

Show the answer

Roles definition, provision, review, deprovision.

R2What is privilege creep?

Show the answer

Accumulating permissions over time as roles change.

R3What does a mover need?

Show the answer

New access and removal of the old access.

R4What is an orphaned account?

Show the answer

An account with no active owner.

R5What does SSO provide?

Show the answer

One login for many applications.

R6Do bots need a life cycle?

Show the answer

Yes, like human users: owner, least privilege, review, removal.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Life cycle roles definition, provision, review, deprovision
Joiner, mover, leaver grant on hire, swap on move, remove on exit
Problems privilege creep, orphaned, dormant, shared accounts
Nonhuman bots and service accounts need owners and review
Tools IAM, directory, SSO, federation, IGA, PAM, MFA
